old: This word is stitched from two pieces: one meaning 'against,' the other meaning 'of life.'
It crossed into English from French, where it already carried the sense of 'against life.'
Break it apart and you get anti- plus -biotic — a name for something opposed to living things, in this case, the small ones that make us sick.
clues: This class of medicine came into English from French, and its name, piece by piece, literally means 'against life'.
A drug, such as penicillin, that kills or halts bacteria inside the body. Unlike an antiseptic wiped on skin, it is swallowed or injected, and it is useless against cold viruses.
Doctors tell you to finish the whole course for strep throat, and they warn that overprescribing these drugs breeds resistant superbugs.
